newsitem.title: USA: Polio cases drop dramatically in Southeast Asia.
newsitem.headline: Polio cases drop dramatically in Southeast Asia.

text.p: Cases of polio have dropped dramatically in Asia during the past decade, offering hope that the illness will be globally eradicated by the year 2000, U.S. federal health officials said on Thursday.

The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said polio cases fell by two-thirds last year in India. Until now, India had reported more than half of the world's polio cases every year. Most of the world's remaining polio cases are in countries in Africa and Southeast Asia.
There were were 1,116 confirmed polio cases in Southeast Asia last year, including 1,005 in India, 63 in Indonesia and 24 in Bangladesh. India had reported 3,263 cases in 1995.

Polio cases in the region have declined 96 percent since 1988, when there were 25,711. Health officials credit intensive immunisation efforts. India immunised 93 million children at the beginning of 1996 and 120 million a year later.
In 1988, the World Health Organisation established a goal of eradicating polio worldwide by the year 2000. "I think we're making excellent progress," Anne-Renee Heningburg of the CDC said.
However, the remaining cases of polio will be harder to eradicate. "They've had two years of National Immunisation Days in India and still they have cases being reported," Heningburg said.
"Probably there are pockets of people who they're still not reaching. That's where they're going to have to really concentrate their efforts," she said.
In the early 1970s, only one in 20 infants were immunised against polio. The worldwide immunisation rate has now risen to 83 percent, the WHO said.

Polio was eradicated from the Western Hemisphere in 1991. The last case was a 3-year-old boy from Peru. As of the end of last year, 97 countries worldwide had conducted at least one round of National Immunisation Days.

Tracking polio is more difficult in Africa, where National Immunisation Days began last year. "The surveillance is just really starting to pick up in Africa so it's hard to know if you have not many cases because you have poor surveillance or whether you have not many cases because there really aren't any," Heningburg said.
